title: Zardari Claims Pakistan's Hindus Prefer 'Being With Us,' Invokes Akhand Bharat Threat
excerpt: Pakistan's president asserted that the country's Hindu minority is content staying in Pakistan while accusing India of pursuing an ideology of undivided India — claims that contrast sharply with documented reports of minority persecution.
body:
• Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari has claimed that the country's Hindu minority prefers living in Pakistan, asserting they would rather be "with us" than in India
  • Zardari accused India of pursuing "Akhand Bharat" — the ideology of an undivided India — framing it as an expansionist threat to Pakistan's sovereignty
  • The remarks come amid continued reports of persecution of Hindus in Pakistan, including forced conversions, abductions, and the destruction of temples in Sindh and other provinces
  • India has previously rejected Zardari's commentary on its internal affairs, with the Ministry of External Affairs calling his remarks "absurd" and highlighting Pakistan's own record on minority rights

Zardari's Claims on Hindu Minority

Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari has claimed that the country's Hindu population prefers "being with us," asserting that Pakistan's Hindu minority is content living in the Islamic republic rather than in neighboring India. In the same remarks, Zardari accused India of believing in "Akhand Bharat" — the concept of an undivided India that encompasses present-day Pakistan and Bangladesh — positioning it as a threat to Pakistan's territorial integrity.

The statements, reported by multiple Indian outlets including Hindustan Times, Outlook India, India Today, and National Herald, come at a time of heightened tensions between the two nuclear-armed neighbors and continuing reports of minority persecution within Pakistan.

The Reality for Pakistan's Hindus

Zardari's portrayal of a content Hindu minority stands in stark contrast to the well-documented difficulties faced by Hindus in Pakistan. The community, estimated at roughly 2 to 4 million people concentrated primarily in Sindh province, has long reported forced conversions, abductions of young women, destruction of temples, and systematic discrimination.

Human rights organizations and Pakistan's own Human Rights Commission have documented a steady outflow of Hindu families to India. According to data cited in Pakistan's National Assembly, approximately 5,000 Hindus migrate from Pakistan to India each year. Many cite religious persecution, kidnapping for ransom, and forced marriages as their primary reasons for leaving.

India's Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019 specifically created a pathway for persecuted religious minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan — including Hindus — to obtain Indian citizenship, a move Pakistan has repeatedly criticized.

India's Sharp Response to Earlier Remarks

Zardari has a pattern of making provocative statements about India's internal affairs. In June 2026, he alleged threats to historic Muslim religious sites in India, prompting a sharp rebuke from India's Ministry of External Affairs.

"India categorically rejects the unwarranted comments made by the President of Pakistan. He has, in any case, no locus standi to comment on matters that are internal to India."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson, June 2026

The MEA called the remarks "particularly absurd given Pakistan's own abysmal record on human rights, which is a matter of global commentary," and described Pakistan's history of "systematically targeting and victimising minorities across various faiths" as "notorious."

In June 2025, Zardari had similarly warned PPP leaders about "growing Hindu extremism" in India, calling it a threat to regional peace — a statement that also drew criticism from Indian observers.

The Akhand Bharat Dimension

The concept of Akhand Bharat — literally "undivided India" — has deep roots in the ideology of Hindu nationalist organizations like the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). While BJP-affiliated leaders have periodically invoked the idea, India's government has never adopted it as official policy. Pakistani leaders, however, have frequently cited it to frame India as an existential threat.

Zardari's invocation of Akhand Bharat alongside his claims about Pakistan's Hindus appears aimed at a domestic audience, reinforcing the narrative of India as an expansionist neighbor while deflecting scrutiny of Pakistan's own minority rights record.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, Zardari's remarks carry particular resonance. Many Indian-Americans trace their roots to regions now in Pakistan, and the plight of Pakistan's Hindu minority remains a deeply personal issue across diaspora communities. Organizations like the American Hindu Coalition and the Hindu American Foundation have repeatedly raised concerns about the declining Hindu population in Pakistan — from roughly 15 percent at the time of Partition in 1947 to under 2 percent today.

The gap between Zardari's assertion that Hindus "prefer being with us" and the documented reality of their experiences is likely to intensify diaspora advocacy around minority rights in Pakistan and fuel further debate about the international community's response to religious persecution in the region.
